editorial:
The Eagle was Rudolph Valentino's penultimate film, released in November 1925 â€” nine months before his death at thirty-one. Produced by Art Finance Corporation (copyright LP22011) and distributed through United Artists, it adapts Aleksandr Pushkin's unfinished 1841 novel Dubrovsky into a Cossack swashbuckler set in Catherine the Great's Russia. Valentino plays Vladimir Dubrovsky, a cavalry officer who becomes the outlaw 'Black Eagle' to avenge his father's dispossession while romancing the daughter of the man who wronged him. The film was photographed by George Barnes, production-designed by William Cameron Menzies, and features a young Gary Cooper in an uncredited bit part as a masked Cossack.

For creators, the 1925 print is public domain in the US by term expiry â€” five years inside the pre-1930 bright line, with registration LP22011 confirmed and no renewal capable of surviving the 1909 Act's 56-year ceiling. The Pushkin source (1841) is equally free. The rights trap is the score: this is a silent film made for live musical accompaniment, so every modern copy adds a separately copyrighted recording. Kino Lorber's Blu-ray edition carries a licensed score and its own digital-fixation copyright; Cohen Media Group holds the 35mm Rohauer print and may produce inquiries even for legally free uses. A reuser who needs a score-free version must locate a raw silent print and verify the specific copy's accompaniment before incorporating any audio.
faq: Can I edit or redistribute the 1925 film footage?

Yes â€” the underlying 1925 film (images, intertitles, performances) is public domain in the US by term expiry. Art Finance Corporation's copyright LP22011 lapsed long before any renewal could have extended it, and the pre-1930 bright line removes any ambiguity. You can cut, redistribute, or remix the footage freely. The one catch is audio: any musical score on the copy you source is a separately copyrighted work. Confirm the specific accompaniment's license â€” or strip the audio â€” before including it in your project.
Does Cohen Media Group's ownership of the Rohauer 35mm print affect my right to use the film?

No. Owning a physical film print does not confer copyright in the underlying work. Raymond Rohauer was notorious for asserting copyright claims on public-domain silent films, and courts generally rejected those claims for pre-1928 works. Cohen Media Group inherited that print collection; they hold property rights in the physical elements, not copyright in the 1925 film. Any genuine new digital restoration Cohen produces carries its own thin fixation copyright â€” but the 1925 footage remains free to use regardless of who owns the surviving print.
